title: Syndrome-as-Header: A Quantum Label-Switching Architecture via Uncorrectable Error Injection
authors: IlKwon Sohn, Ju-Bong Kim, Kwangil Bae, Wooyeong Song, Wonhyuk Lee
abstract: Scaling quantum networks beyond point-to-point links requires packet forwarding that can tolerate control-plane timing uncertainty. Existing optical-burst switching (OBS) and quantum-wrapper-based packet switching (QW) rely on external classical headers whose jitter-prone processing must remain aligned with in-flight quantum payloads, creating guard-window or fiber-delay-line budget failures. This paper proposes Syndrome-as-Header (SAH), a quantum label-switching architecture that embeds routing labels into the syndrome structure of an encoded payload. The proposed scheme uses Uncorrectable Error Injection (UEI) to map flow labels to reference syndromes and builds a syndrome-space header codebook whose decoding regions remain distinguishable under correctable channel-induced syndrome deviations. Core routers extract the syndrome header, suppress the correctable residual channel-error component, and swap labels without measuring or decoding the logical payload. SAH supports FAST forwarding and VERIFICATION mode, the latter providing end-to-end consistency checking while retaining swappable labels. In NSFNet timing benchmarks with common per-hop quantum error correction (QEC), SAH eliminates the external-header/payload alignment condition, so timing uncertainty appears as memory residence and delivered latency rather than alignment-budget drops. With a $T_2$-based memory-residence penalty, the advantage depends on router memory coherence; for sufficiently long coherence, SAH maintains higher acceptance and throughput than OBS+QEC and QW+QEC under high jitter.
summary: This paper introduces Syndrome-as-Header (SAH), a new quantum label-switching architecture designed to enable scalable quantum networking. SAH embeds routing labels within the syndrome structure of encoded qubits using Uncorrectable Error Injection. This method bypasses critical timing alignment issues inherent in existing protocols, allowing for robust forwarding even under high control-plane jitter.
main_problem: Scaling quantum networks beyond point-to-point links requires packet forwarding that can tolerate control-plane timing uncertainty, which existing methods fail to achieve.
main_result: The proposed Syndrome-as-Header (SAH) architecture eliminates the strict external-header/payload alignment condition by embedding routing labels directly into the syndrome structure of the encoded payload.
method: SAH uses Uncorrectable Error Injection (UEI) to map flow labels to reference syndromes, allowing core routers to swap labels solely by extracting and manipulating the syndrome header without decoding the logical payload.
model_or_system: The system models a quantum label-switching network inspired by MPLS, using qubits encoded via an $[[n, k, d]]$ stabilizer code. Forwarding relies on local per-hop memory residence rather than long-term end-to-end storage.
key_observables: Acceptance probability and throughput under high jitter; delivered latency; syndrome header extraction success rate.
important_parameters: Router memory coherence time ($T_2$); physical error rate per hop ($p_{ch}$); code parameters ($n, k, d$).
main_assumptions: The advantage depends on sufficient router memory coherence ($T_2$); the classical control plane is assumed reliable for distributing label bindings.
figures_summary: Figures compare SAH performance against OBS+QEC and QW+QEC under jitter, showing superior throughput; other figures detail syndrome-space header mapping and mode operation (FAST/VERIFICATION).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the limitations of current quantum packet switching, proposes the SAH mechanism using UEI to embed labels in syndromes, details the FAST and VERIFICATION modes, and validates performance against benchmarks showing timing robustness.
why_interesting: It provides a novel protocol for network routing that integrates directly into the error correction framework, making it highly relevant for quantum communication hardware design where timing jitter is a major bottleneck.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Illustrative comparison of forwarding-header abstractions. (a) An address-dominated classical header carries endpoint address fields, type/control information, and payload. (b) The proposed logical compact header h = (ℓ, q) contains only a flow label and a sequence number, which are mapped via UEI to an admissible reference syndrome sref(h) and embedded across encoded blocks. The comparison highlights compact syndrome-domain forwarding without requiring a classical frame format for quantum packets.

Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed SAH architecture in FAST and VERIFICATION modes. The ingress embeds a per-block compact header h into an encoded block via a UEI labeling operator Elab(h) with reference syndrome sref(h) = f(h) = s(Elab(h)); core routers identify the in-band header, infer the residual channel-error component, apply the corresponding correction, and swap labels without decoding the logical payload. FAST mode performs autonomous label switching using the in-band header and pre-installed swap rules, whereas VERIFICATION mode additionally embeds a flow-specific verification component Ever with sver = s(Ever) and checks it at the egress before payload release.
